question_text: A 28-year-old graduate student visits the university health clinic for 3-weeks of epigastric pain that worsens with meals, associated with retrosternal pain, early satiety, and bloating. Physical examination is only positive for a mild epigastric tenderness. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach in this case?

                    ### Question
                    A 28-year-old graduate student visits the university health clinic for 3-weeks of epigastric pain that worsens with meals, associated with retrosternal pain, early satiety, and bloating. She denies vomiting blood or blood in her stool. She has been consuming large volumes of caffeinated-drinks and fast-food for a month, as she has been studying for her tests. Her family and personal history are unremarkable with no history of gastrointestinal cancer. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination is only positive for a mild epigastric tenderness. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach in this case?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Upper endoscopy
opb. Barium swallow radiograph
opc. Fecal antigen testing for Helicobacter pylori
opd. Treatment with omeprazole
ope. Treatment with metoclopramide

The patient presents with epigastric pain worsening with meals, retrosternal pain, early satiety, and bloating, likely indicating gastritis or peptic ulcer disease, especially given her recent high intake of caffeinated drinks and fast food. Fecal antigen testing for Helicobacter pylori is a non-invasive and appropriate initial approach to assess for this common cause of gastritis. While omeprazole is effective for managing gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and could provide symptomatic relief, it is more appropriate to first confirm the presence of H. pylori before initiating treatment. Upper endoscopy is not warranted at this stage due to the absence of alarming symptoms, and barium swallow is less useful for this presentation. Metoclopramide is not first-line for these symptoms. Therefore, the best approach is fecal antigen testing for H. pylori.
